nameStory: The Autumn Meadowhawk gets its name from its peak flying season in late summer and fall, when most other dragonflies have called it quits for the year. These hardy fliers patrol meadows, fields, and other open spaces well into October, earning them their seasonal moniker. They're also called Yellow-legged Meadowhawks for their distinctive bright yellow legs that look like tiny golden stilts.
description: The Autumn Meadowhawk is a medium-sized dragonfly that grows about 1-1.5 inches long, making it roughly the size of a large paperclip. Males sport bright red bodies that gleam like tiny rubies in the sunlight, while females are more golden-yellow or tan colored. Like all dragonflies, they have four clear wings that they hold out perpendicular to their body when perched, and enormous compound eyes that take up most of their head. These are the dragonflies you're most likely to see on warm autumn days when other insects have disappeared.

idTips.label: Bright yellow legs
idTips.description: Look for legs that are bright golden-yellow from top to bottom - they're so vivid they almost glow in sunlight and feel smooth and thin if you gently handle a deceased specimen

idTips.label: Red male coloration
idTips.description: Mature males develop a brilliant cherry-red abdomen and thorax that looks almost metallic in bright light, while young males and females remain yellowish-brown

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with no dark patches or bands, and make a distinctive papery rustling sound when they take off from their perch

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About the length of your thumb from tip to first joint, with a sturdy build that feels substantial but delicate if handled

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perching on bare twigs, fence posts, or tall grass stems in full sun, returning repeatedly to the same favorite spots

habitat: Autumn Meadowhawks thrive around still or slow-moving water like ponds, marshes, boggy areas, and quiet stream backwaters where they lay their eggs. You'll spot the adults hunting in nearby open areas - meadows, fields, gardens, and sunny woodland clearings where they patrol for small flying insects. They prefer areas with scattered perches like fence posts, dead branches, or tall weeds where they can rest between hunting flights.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active in spring, though eggs laid the previous fall are developing underwater in ponds and marshes.
seasonality.summer: Young adults begin emerging from water in mid to late summer, with females and immature males showing yellowish coloration before males develop their red breeding colors.
seasonality.fall: Peak activity time when mature red males are most visible, actively mating and laying eggs. They remain active well into October, often the last dragonflies you'll see before winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, leaving behind eggs that will overwinter underwater and hatch into aquatic nymphs in spring.

funFact: Autumn Meadowhawks can actually raise their body temperature by rapidly vibrating their flight muscles while perched, allowing them to stay active on cool autumn mornings when other insects are too sluggish to fly - essentially giving themselves a warm-up workout before takeoff!
confusionNotes: The biggest mix-up is with other red meadowhawks, especially the Ruby Meadowhawk, but Autumn Meadowhawks have bright yellow legs while Ruby Meadowhawks have black legs. Memory trick: 'Autumn leaves are yellow, autumn dragonfly legs are yellow.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Yellow-legged Meadowhawk' in some field guides, most people know them as Autumn Meadowhawks because they're so strongly associated with fall weather. The scientific name 'vicinum' means 'neighboring' or 'nearby,' possibly referring to how common and widespread they are in suitable habitats.
compareHints: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, Autumn Meadowhawks are distinguished by their completely yellow legs - most other meadowhawks have black legs or black stripes on their legs. The White-faced Meadowhawk has a distinctive white face (as the name suggests), while the Band-winged Meadowhawk has dark bands across its wings that Autumn Meadowhawks lack entirely.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England meadowhawks, the band-winged is the only one with prominent dark wing bands - ruby meadowhawks have clear wings and bright red males, while autumn meadowhawks lack wing bands and have more orange-red coloring.
Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, the white-faced is the only one where males develop a pure white face - other meadowhawks have reddish, yellowish, or dark faces.

Among New England's meadowhawks, the Saffron-winged is most easily distinguished by its golden wing stripes in younger individuals and females, while the Ruby Meadowhawk typically shows clearer wings and the White-faced has a distinctly pale face.

Cherry-faced meadowhawks are distinguished from other meadowhawks primarily by their very dark red, almost burgundy faces when mature, compared to the brighter reds of ruby meadowhawks or the white faces of white-faced meadowhawks.
